chunks: "The buck shows up wherever you have a higher voltage and need a lower one efficiently.
The most common case is point-of-load rails on a board: a 12 volts or 5 volts rail stepped down to 3. 3, 1. 8, 1. 2 or even 0. 9 volts for processors, FPGAs and memory.
Anything battery powered is another big one. A Li-ion cell at 3. 7 volts feeding a 1.
8 volts microcontroller is better served by a buck than an LDO because the efficiency, and so the runtime, is much higher. Then there are the high-power ones.
A CPU or GPU core rail is a multiphase buck taking 12 volts down to about 1 volts at tens or hundreds of amps, because a linear regulator at that current would be a heater.
Automotive and industrial 12, 24 or 48 volts buses get bucked down to 5 volts or 3. 3 volts logic rails, and drone or robot batteries get bucked to 5 volts for the compute board.
The same power stage also regulates current instead of voltage: LED drivers, battery chargers, and solar MPPT charge controllers are all buck-based.
I'd pick an LDO instead when the dropout is tiny, the load is very light, or the rail is noise-sensitive.
A common compromise is a buck for the bulk drop followed by an LDO for a clean analog rail."
